current_episode.title: The Otago Opportunity - Episode 22 - Workforce Central Dunedin

guest.bio_context: Raymond Clark is trained as a primary school teacher and previously worked at the Department of Corrections before pivoting into the role of Operations Manager for Workforce Central Dunedin. He has led the job and skills hub since its inception around 2017-2018, becoming active on the Dunedin Hospital build in 2020. Under his leadership, Workforce Central Dunedin has placed 312 people into employment and trained approximately 1,300 people in various skills.

context.transcript_excerpt: Coming up on the Otago Opportunity, we're talking to Raymond Clark from Workforce Central Dunedin. This is the Otago Opportunity, a limited series look at the future of our province. I'm your host Pauline Moore and in this series we're taking the policies of the Opportunity Party and moving them out of the Wellington think tank and into our own backyard here in Dunedin. Each week we'll hear from local business owners, students and families about how a tax reset or a citizens' assembly would actually impact their daily lives. It's not about the politics, it's about the future of the place we call home. Welcome to the Otago Opportunity. Kia ora and welcome to the Otago Opportunity. Joining me today is Dave Bainbridge-Zaffa, the Opportunity Candidate for Dunedin. Welcome Dave. Kia ora. and our guest, Raymond Clark, the Operations Manager for Workforce Central Dunedin. Kia ora, everyone. Thanks for taking the time to talk to us, Raymond. Can you start maybe by just telling us a little bit about what Workforce Central Dunedin is and why it was created? Yes, certainly. Workforce Central Dunedin was first conceptualised in about 2017-2018 by the people who were looking ahead at the workforce needs of the new Dunedin Hospital build. And they decided, and it was worked out, that of the critical risks that were facing the construction of the hospital, workforce shortages was going to be one of the major critical risks, one of four. So they established Workforce Central as a job and skills hub. We're the only job and skills hub in South Island. And there are many, probably as many as seven or eight up in Auckland and around the North Island. But we're the only one here. And the Job and Skills Hub basically is designed to get locals into the opportunities that are created by the hospital build. So we want locals to get those jobs. We want locals to get entry level apprenticeships. and we want local businesses to become supply chain partners and to service the contractors on the hospital building. And had you done this before, this sort of thing? I have not done any work on a job and skills hub before. Every day that comes to me is a brand new day that I haven't had before. I'm trained as a primary school teacher and I previously worked at the Department of Corrections and I pivoted into Job and Skills Hub. So I was brand new. And so did you model it on something else or how did you start? So the concept was modelled on a Job and Skills Hub over in Sydney in a place called Bangaroo. And obviously it was quite likely modelled on the Job and Skills Hub at the Auckland airport. And just in terms of its concept and design. But once I started, I was able to take the Job and Skills Hub in the direction of my skill set and in the direction of the things that I thought was correct for what we were doing. And obviously, we were governed by MB, who had an overarching contract, and we had to fulfill the requirements of the contract. But how those requirements were fulfilled was entirely up to myself and the other people in the hub. So how did that go? What were the challenges? Oh, look, we had lots of challenges. First of all, we were kicked off in 2020, and the outpatients build was supposed to start sometime later in 2020. And as we got close to the time, it was delayed and delayed and delayed. And eventually, the outpatients build started only, well, three and a half years ago now. And the inpatients build only started in July last year. So the alignment of the job and skills hub and the build that we were supposed to serve was completely out of whack. And so we had to go around and look at other industries in Dunedin and do our work in terms of supplying workforce and supplying coordinated training needs and postural care and things like that to other areas, to other parts of the construction industry around Dunedin and to hospitality even. pending_qa.q: How did Workforce Central Dunedin adapt when the hospital construction was delayed?
pending_qa.r: The outpatients build was delayed significantly and only started three and a half years ago, while the inpatients build started in July of the previous year. Because of this misalignment, Workforce Central Dunedin pivoted to work with other industries in Dunedin, supplying workforce and coordinated training to other parts of the construction industry and hospitality. Clark states: 'We put lots of people into jobs that had got nothing to do with construction because there we were and we were working and we needed to do something.' This diversification actually provided significant benefits, allowing the organization to build connections across industries.

pending_qa.q: What is the return on investment for Workforce Central Dunedin's training and employment services?
pending_qa.r: A local consultant calculated a return on investment of five to one, based on the number of people taken off benefits and placed into work, their economic contribution, and the cost of coordinated or delivered training. Raymond Clark states: 'We had a local consultant who calculated a return of five to one, being the amount of people that we've taken off the benefit, the amount of people that we've put into work and their input back into the economy.'

pending_qa.q: What challenges exist in training apprentices on time-limited construction contracts?
pending_qa.r: Contractors struggle to take on apprentices because the average lifespan of contracts on the hospital build is about eight months, and contractors may not have work ahead to continue employing apprentices after their contract ends. This structural characteristic of the industry creates strong reliance on overseas labour, mostly from the Philippines. Despite maximizing opportunities for entry-level roles, apprentices placed were countable on two hands and laborers were less than 40.

pending_qa.q: What pastoral care and mental health services does Workforce Central Dunedin provide on site?
pending_qa.r: Workforce Central Dunedin provides a workplace nurse who visits once weekly to screen workers for blood pressure, eye testing, and muscle pain. The organization partnered with Mates in Construction, a suicide awareness initiative, and co-located them in the office. Additional services include physiotherapy through university student partnerships at low fees, onsite barber services (with donations given to charity), and mental health support. The organization has been a finalist in the SightSafe Awards twice: once for pastoral care and once for cultural competency training developed for the Philippine community.

pending_qa.q: How many people has Workforce Central Dunedin placed into employment and trained?
pending_qa.r: Over five and a half years of operation, with three and a half years active on the hospital build, Workforce Central Dunedin has placed 312 people into employment and trained or upskilled approximately 1,300 people through training such as Site Safe, scaffolding work, and cultural awareness courses.

pending_qa.q: What awards and recognition has Workforce Central Dunedin received?
pending_qa.r: Workforce Central Dunedin won an award from Kuma, a Māori business collective, for being their best business partner. The organization was also a finalist in the SightSafe Awards on two occasions—once for pastoral care and once for cultural competency—and received the judges' choice award as a finalist for the Good Youth Employer Award.

pending_qa.q: What is the size difference between the outpatients and inpatients builds of Dunedin Hospital?
pending_qa.r: The inpatients build is approximately five times the size of the outpatients build in terms of floor space and will be 11 stories high. This larger scale presents significantly greater opportunities for workforce placement and training compared to the outpatients phase.

pending_qa.q: What funding challenges does Workforce Central Dunedin face after the hospital build completes?
pending_qa.r: The MB funding ended in December last year, with MBIE having been clear that the funding was seed funding and would not continue. Workforce Central Dunedin currently operates on limited MSD funding ending in July next year and a fee-for-service model where they receive a small percentage of hourly rates for placements. Raymond Clark states the organization faces 'existential pressure' because contractors previously received free services and now must pay, while the fit-out phase—where most jobs will be created—does not start until after the MSD funding ends.

pending_qa.q: What legislative change does Raymond Clark recommend to strengthen social procurement outcomes in New Zealand?
pending_qa.r: Raymond Clark advocates for converting social procurement rules into law rather than policy. He notes that in Australia and Canada, social procurement is law and companies must deliver on those outcomes. In New Zealand, social procurement is policy, so if companies cannot deliver, no one monitors compliance. He states: 'There's no funds to do that. They've hardly got the funds to build a proper hospital, never mind have social procurement as well.' He calls for government funding to support social procurement requirements and for someone to monitor implementation.
